# Introduction

This assignment communicates findings from my **Group Project data** in two ways:

1. **Project 1:** a **static dashboard** built with Quarto and published on GitHub Pages
2. **Project 2:** an **interactive Shiny app** published on shinyapps.io

Each project tells a different story. The static dashboard answers one focused question with a clear takeaway. The Shiny app lets the audience explore the data themselves.

::: {.callout-note}
## About the data

Both projects use the Shopify e-commerce dataset from our Group Project (Group 2): **60,000 orders** placed between **January 1, 2023 and June 18, 2025**, with 17 variables describing the product, discount, customer country, marketing channel, payment method, return status, rating, revenue, and profit.
:::

# Project 1: Static Dashboard with Quarto

## Project Description

**Story: "Do discounts pay off?"**

Almost **9 out of 10 orders** in this store used a discount, ranging from 5% to 40%. A common assumption in e-commerce is that discounts encourage customers to buy more. This dashboard tests that assumption by comparing order size, order value, and returns at each discount level.

The dashboard has three pages:

| Page | Purpose |
|:--|:--|
| **Overview** | Headline numbers (value boxes), the monthly revenue trend, and a plain-English summary |
| **Discounts** | The core story: items per order, order value, and return rate at each discount level |
| **Channels & Categories** | Context: revenue by traffic source and product category |

: Structure of the static dashboard {#tbl-dash-pages}

## Data Description

| Variable | Type | Description |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `order_date` | Date | Date the order was placed |
| `product_category` | Categorical (7) | Accessories, Beauty, Electronics, Fashion, Footwear, Home Decor, Sports |
| `product_price` | Numeric | List price of the product (\$5–\$800) |
| `discount_percent` | Numeric | Discount applied: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, or 40% |
| `quantity` | Numeric | Items in the order (1–5) |
| `traffic_source` | Categorical (5) | Direct, Email, Organic, Paid Ads, Social Media |
| `customer_country` | Categorical (7) | Australia, Canada, Germany, India, UAE, UK, USA |
| `payment_method` | Categorical (5) | Apple Pay, Cash on Delivery, Credit Card, Debit Card, PayPal |
| `is_returned` | Binary | 1 if the order was returned |
| `rating` | Numeric | Customer rating (1–5) |
| `revenue` | Numeric | Discounted price × quantity |
| `profit` | Numeric | Revenue minus shipping cost |

: Key variables used in both dashboards {#tbl-vars}

## R Code

The complete source of the dashboard (`shopify-dashboard.qmd`), including the YAML header:

````r
---
title: "Do Discounts Pay Off? Shopify Sales 2023–2025"
author: "Alexa Bueno"
format:
  dashboard:
    theme: cosmo
    orientation: rows
    nav-buttons:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/Buenoalexa11/IBM6540-Reports
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

sales <- read_csv("shopify_sales_dataset_ml_eda.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    order_date = as.Date(order_date),
    month      = floor_date(order_date, "month"),
    list_value = product_price * quantity,
    discount_band = factor(paste0(discount_percent, "%"),
                           levels = paste0(sort(unique(discount_percent)), "%"))
  )

by_discount <- sales |>
  group_by(discount_band) |>
  summarise(
    orders       = n(),
    avg_quantity = mean(quantity),
    avg_order    = mean(revenue),
    return_rate  = mean(is_returned),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

full_price_aov <- by_discount$avg_order[by_discount$discount_band == "0%"]
deep_disc_aov  <- by_discount$avg_order[by_discount$discount_band == "40%"]
discount_given <- sum(sales$list_value - sales$revenue)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
```

# Overview

## Row {height=22%}

```{r}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Total revenue"
list(icon = "currency-dollar", color = "primary",

```

```{r}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Orders"
list(icon = "cart", color = "info", value = comma(nrow(sales)))
```

```{r}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Average order value"
list(icon = "receipt", color = "success", value = dollar(mean(sales$revenue), accuracy = 1))
```

```{r}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Given away in discounts"
list(icon = "tag", color = "warning",
     value = paste0("$", round(discount_given / 1e6, 1), "M"))
```

## Row {height=78%}

### Column {width=65%}

```{r}
#| title: "Monthly revenue (June 2025 is a partial month)"
sales |>
  count(month, wt = revenue, name = "revenue") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, revenue)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2780e3", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#2780e3", size = 1.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Revenue")
```

### Column {width=35%}

::: {.card title="What is this dashboard about?"}
This dashboard uses **60,000 Shopify orders** placed between **January 2023 and June 2025** across 7 product categories, 7 countries, and 5 traffic sources.

**The question:** almost 9 out of 10 orders used a discount. *Do those discounts actually get customers to buy more?*

**The short answer:** no. Customers buy about **3 items per order whether the discount is 0% or 40%**, so deeper discounts simply shrink the order value. See the **Discounts** tab for the details.
:::

# Discounts

## Row {height=50%}

```{r}
#| title: "Items per order barely moves with the discount"
ggplot(by_discount, aes(discount_band, avg_quantity)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3fb618") +
  geom_text(aes(label = number(avg_quantity, accuracy = 0.01)), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 3.5)) +
  labs(x = "Discount", y = "Average items per order")
```

```{r}
#| title: "But the average order value falls with every discount step"
ggplot(by_discount, aes(discount_band, avg_order)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#ff7518") +
  geom_text(aes(label = dollar(avg_order, accuracy = 1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(), limits = c(0, 1350)) +
  labs(x = "Discount", y = "Average revenue per order")
```

## Row {height=50%}

```{r}
#| title: "Return rate by discount level"
ggplot(by_discount, aes(discount_band, return_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#9954bb") +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(return_rate, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(), limits = c(0, 0.18)) +
  labs(x = "Discount", y = "Share of orders returned")
```

::: {.card title="How to read this page"}
- **Top left:** a 40% discount does **not** lead to bigger baskets. Customers buy about **3 items** at every discount level.
- **Top right:** because quantity stays flat, each discount step lowers the order value. Orders fall from **`r dollar(full_price_aov, accuracy = 1)`** at full price to **`r dollar(deep_disc_aov, accuracy = 1)`** at 40% off, a drop of **`r percent(1 - deep_disc_aov / full_price_aov, accuracy = 1)`**.
- **Bottom left:** deeper discounts also come with slightly *more* returns.

**Takeaway:** in this store, discounts reduce revenue without increasing how much people buy. Testing smaller or more targeted discounts could protect margin.
:::

# Channels & Categories

## Row

```{r}
#| title: "Revenue by traffic source"
sales |>
  count(traffic_source, wt = revenue, name = "revenue") |>
  ggplot(aes(revenue, fct_reorder(traffic_source, revenue))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2780e3") +
  geom_text(aes(label = dollar(revenue, scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M", accuracy = 0.1)),
            hjust = 1.1, color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  labs(x = "Revenue", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| title: "Revenue and return rate by product category"
sales |>
  group_by(product_category) |>
  summarise(revenue = sum(revenue), return_rate = mean(is_returned)) |>
  ggplot(aes(revenue, fct_reorder(product_category, revenue))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3fb618") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(percent(return_rate, accuracy = 0.1), " returned")),
            hjust = 1.1, color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  labs(x = "Revenue", y = NULL)
```

## Row {height=25%}

::: {.card title="What this page shows"}
Revenue is spread **almost evenly** across all five traffic sources (about 20% each) and all seven product categories, and the return rate stays near **15%** everywhere. No single channel or category is carrying the business. That makes the **discount policy** the clearest lever for improving revenue.
:::
````

## Findings from the Data

### Interpreting the Dashboard Charts

**Overview page**

- The store earned about **\$59.6M** in revenue from **60,000 orders**, with an average order value of about **\$994**.
- About **\$13.2M** was given away in discounts, roughly 18% of what the same orders would have cost at full price.
- Monthly revenue is **stable at roughly \$1.7M–\$2.1M**. The sharp drop at the end is only because June 2025 is a partial month (data ends June 18).

**Discounts page (the main story)**

- **Items per order do not change with the discount.** Customers buy about **3.0 items** whether they get 0% or 40% off.
- Because baskets don't grow, **every discount step lowers the order value**: from **\$1,202** at full price to **\$721** at 40% off, a **40% drop**.
- Return rates rise slightly with deeper discounts, from **14.1%** at full price to **15.4%** at 40% off.

**Channels & Categories page**

- Revenue is spread almost evenly across the **five traffic sources (about 20% each)** and the **seven product categories (about \$8.3M–\$8.7M each)**.
- Return rates sit close to **15%** in every category.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key takeaway

In this store, **discounts reduce revenue without increasing how much customers buy**. Since no single channel or category stands out, the discount policy is the clearest lever for improving revenue. A next step would be A/B testing smaller or more targeted discounts.
:::

# Project 2: Interactive Shiny App

## Project Description

**Story: "Explore the business yourself."**

The static dashboard answers one question. Managers usually have their own questions, though: *How did Paid Ads do last quarter? Which country has the most returns? Are ratings trending down?* The **Shopify Sales Explorer** app lets any user answer questions like these without writing code.

The app lets the audience:

- **Filter by date range** to focus on a season, year, or campaign period
- **Select different variables:** choose the metric (revenue, profit, orders, average order value, return rate, or average rating) and what to compare it by (traffic source, product category, country, or payment method)
- **Explore trends interactively:** switch between weekly, monthly, and quarterly views, show or hide individual groups, hover for exact values, and zoom into the trend chart

## Data Description

The app uses the same Shopify dataset described in @tbl-vars. All metrics are recalculated live from the order-level data each time the user changes a filter:

| Metric | Calculation |
|:--|:--|
| Revenue | Sum of `revenue` |
| Profit | Sum of `profit` |
| Orders | Number of orders |
| Average order value | Mean of `revenue` |
| Return rate | Mean of `is_returned` |
| Average rating | Mean of `rating` |

: Metrics available in the Shiny app {#tbl-metrics}

## R Code

The complete Shiny app (`app.R`). It is built with `bslib` for the layout, `dplyr` for the reactive summaries, and `ggplot2` + `plotly` for the interactive charts.

````r
# Shopify Sales Explorer: interactive Shiny app
# Alexa Bueno | IBM 6540 W07-M10 Dashboards Assignment

library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(scales)

# ---- Data -------------------------------------------------------------------
sales <- read_csv("shopify_sales_dataset_ml_eda.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(order_date = as.Date(order_date))

breakdowns <- c(
  "Traffic source"   = "traffic_source",
  "Product category" = "product_category",
  "Country"          = "customer_country",
  "Payment method"   = "payment_method"
)

metrics <- c(
  "Revenue"             = "revenue",
  "Profit"              = "profit",
  "Orders"              = "orders",
  "Average order value" = "aov",
  "Return rate"         = "return_rate",
  "Average rating"      = "rating"
)

# Summarise every metric for whatever grouping is passed in
summarise_metrics <- function(df) {
  df |>
    summarise(
      revenue     = sum(revenue),
      profit      = sum(profit),
      orders      = n(),
      aov         = mean(revenue),
      return_rate = mean(is_returned),
      rating      = mean(rating),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

# Pick the right number format for each metric
metric_label <- function(metric) {
  switch(metric,
    revenue     = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()),
    profit      = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()),
    aov         = label_dollar(),
    return_rate = label_percent(accuracy = 0.1),
    rating      = label_number(accuracy = 0.01),
    label_comma()
  )
}

# ---- UI ---------------------------------------------------------------------
ui <- page_sidebar(
  title = "Shopify Sales Explorer (2023–2025)",
  theme = bs_theme(bootswatch = "cosmo"),

  sidebar = sidebar(
    width = 300,
    dateRangeInput("dates", "Date range",
                   start = min(sales$order_date), end = max(sales$order_date),
                   min   = min(sales$order_date), max = max(sales$order_date)),
    selectInput("metric", "Metric", choices = metrics, selected = "revenue"),
    selectInput("breakdown", "Compare by", choices = breakdowns,
                selected = "traffic_source"),
    selectizeInput("groups", "Show these groups", choices = NULL, multiple = TRUE),
    radioButtons("grain", "Time grouping",
                 choices = c("Week" = "week", "Month" = "month", "Quarter" = "quarter"),
                 selected = "month", inline = TRUE),
    hr(),
    p(class = "small text-muted",
      "Data: 60,000 Shopify orders, Jan 2023 – Jun 2025 (IBM 6540 Group Project).")
  ),

  layout_columns(
    fill = FALSE,
    value_box("Revenue",             textOutput("vb_revenue"), theme = "primary"),
    value_box("Orders",              textOutput("vb_orders"),  theme = "info"),
    value_box("Average order value", textOutput("vb_aov"),     theme = "success"),
    value_box("Return rate",         textOutput("vb_return"),  theme = "warning")
  ),

  layout_columns(
    col_widths = c(8, 4),
    card(card_header(textOutput("trend_title")), plotlyOutput("trend")),
    card(card_header(textOutput("bar_title")),   plotlyOutput("bars"))
  ),

  card(
    card_header("How to use this app"),
    p("This app lets you explore how a Shopify store's sales change over time and across marketing channels,",
      "product categories, countries, and payment methods."),
    tags$ol(
      tags$li(strong("Pick a date range"), " to focus on a season, a year, or a campaign period."),
      tags$li(strong("Pick a metric"), " such as revenue, return rate, or average rating."),
      tags$li(strong("Pick what to compare"), " and choose which groups to show."),
      tags$li("Hover over the charts to see exact values. Drag on the trend chart to zoom in.")
    )
  )
)

# ---- Server -----------------------------------------------------------------
server <- function(input, output, session) {

  # Refresh the group choices whenever the breakdown changes
  observeEvent(input$breakdown, {
    choices <- sort(unique(sales[[input$breakdown]]))
    updateSelectizeInput(session, "groups", choices = choices, selected = choices)
  })

  filtered <- reactive({
    req(input$dates, input$groups)
    sales |>
      filter(order_date >= input$dates[1],
             order_date <= input$dates[2],
             .data[[input$breakdown]] %in% input$groups)
  })

  metric_name    <- reactive(names(metrics)[metrics == input$metric])
  breakdown_name <- reactive(names(breakdowns)[breakdowns == input$breakdown])

  # Value boxes
  totals <- reactive({
    validate(need(nrow(filtered()) > 0, "No orders match these filters."))
    summarise_metrics(filtered())
  })
  output$vb_revenue <- renderText(dollar(totals()$revenue, scale_cut = cut_short_scale()))
  output$vb_orders  <- renderText(comma(totals()$orders))
  output$vb_aov     <- renderText(dollar(totals()$aov, accuracy = 1))
  output$vb_return  <- renderText(percent(totals()$return_rate, accuracy = 0.1))

  output$trend_title <- renderText(paste(metric_name(), "over time by", tolower(breakdown_name())))
  output$bar_title   <- renderText(paste(metric_name(), "by", tolower(breakdown_name())))

  # Trend chart
  output$trend <- renderPlotly({
    validate(need(nrow(filtered()) > 0, "No orders match these filters."))
    trend <- filtered() |>
      mutate(period = floor_date(order_date, input$grain),
             group  = .data[[input$breakdown]]) |>
      group_by(period, group) |>
      summarise_metrics()

    p <- ggplot(trend, aes(period, .data[[input$metric]], color = group,
                           text = paste0(group, "<br>", period, "<br>",
                                         metric_label(input$metric)(.data[[input$metric]])))) +
      geom_line(aes(group = group)) +
      scale_y_continuous(labels = metric_label(input$metric)) +
      labs(x = NULL, y = metric_name(), color = breakdown_name()) +
      theme_minimal()

    ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
  })

  # Bar chart
  output$bars <- renderPlotly({
    validate(need(nrow(filtered()) > 0, "No orders match these filters."))
    bars <- filtered() |>
      mutate(group = .data[[input$breakdown]]) |>
      group_by(group) |>
      summarise_metrics() |>
      mutate(group = reorder(group, .data[[input$metric]]))

    p <- ggplot(bars, aes(.data[[input$metric]], group,
                          text = metric_label(input$metric)(.data[[input$metric]]))) +
      geom_col(fill = "#2780e3") +
      scale_x_continuous(labels = metric_label(input$metric)) +
      labs(x = metric_name(), y = NULL) +
      theme_minimal()

    ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
````

### How the App Works

- **UI:** `page_sidebar()` puts all inputs in a sidebar, with four value boxes and two chart cards in the main panel.
- **Reactivity:** `filtered()` is a reactive expression that re-filters the data whenever the dates, comparison variable, or groups change. Every output depends on it, so the whole app updates together.
- **Dynamic inputs:** `observeEvent()` refreshes the "Show these groups" list whenever the user changes the "Compare by" variable.
- **Interactivity:** `ggplotly()` turns each `ggplot` into an interactive chart with hover tooltips and zoom.

## Key Findings from the Data

### Interpreting the Dashboard Charts

Exploring the app with different settings shows:

- **Trend chart:** with *Revenue* by *Traffic source* at a monthly grain, all five channels move closely together, mostly between about \$350K and \$440K per month. No channel consistently pulls ahead, which suggests the marketing mix is balanced rather than dependent on one source.
- **Bar chart:** each traffic source brings in about \$11.8M–\$12.0M over the full period. Social Media is narrowly the highest and Email narrowly the lowest.
- **Return rate:** switching the metric to *Return rate* and comparing by *Product category* shows Sports and Fashion slightly above the ~15% average, and Home Decor slightly below.
- **Date filtering:** narrowing the date range to 2025 shows the business holding steady, with the apparent June drop again explained by the partial month.

# Conclusion

The two projects show two complementary ways to communicate with data:

- The **static Quarto dashboard** is best for delivering **one clear message**. Here, that message is that discounts lower order value without growing baskets.
- The **interactive Shiny app** is best when the audience has **many different questions**, because it lets them filter, compare, and explore on their own.
